Around three in the small hours the wind and waves eased a little, and a heavy fog rose off the sea; no starlight showed, and the ship seemed to walk in its sleep through a black and boundless world. They were now in the waters of the Zhoushan Archipelago, thick with sunken reefs below, and the ship had slowed to eleven knots; the sea had fallen almost wholly still, and there was only the sound of the waves slapping and scraping along the hull. Out of the darkness a harsh blast of the siren rang all at once, and a light flashed dim and quick in the black — the ship had strayed a little off course and was bearing down on a great spread of reef ahead. She put her helm hard over to starboard, and her stern all but grazed the jagged rocks.

Most of the passengers in the cabins never noticed; a few, at the ship's sudden turn, only rolled over in their berths in their sleep. But Liang Shichao woke. The question he had been turning over before he slept came back to him, and after two or three minutes he said, down toward the lower berth:
“You mean the man who really died on Haoxian Road was Long Dong?”

“At that point, I think, Lu Zhongde did not yet know he would be taking the name of the man he had murdered — which is why he let Uncle Li at the cigarette shop catch sight of him at the Dragon Boat Festival.”

Long Dong had been lured to his death by Lu Zhongde. Little Phoenix was an opera singer, the mainstay of the Qunfangyan troupe, able to hold every line in her memory. She still remembered what Lu Zhongde had said to Long Dong over the telephone: You've already left; you can't go back to that place again. So Long Dong had by then already begun to withdraw. Perhaps the word spoken on the telephone had been precisely “withdraw,” only Little Phoenix was not much used to that way of speaking. When Long Dong was killed, Ouyang Min had been arrested; after the Dragon Boat Festival Ouyang Min turned traitor, and it was only at this point that Ye Qinian decided to have Lu Zhongde pose as Yi Junnian and put false news in the papers.
“So Long Dong was the real Yi Junnian?” Liang Shichao's mind could scarcely keep pace.
Long Dong was the one who should have come to Shanghai that July and made contact with Old Fang. The organization had transferred him from Guangzhou to Shanghai to set up an intelligence network.

“Yi Junnian is a false name, a working alias, one that Comrade Long Dong was meant to use — booking his boat ticket under it, booking the place he would stay in Shanghai. In Shanghai too he would have used this name to make his contacts.”
“And when Lu Zhongde took the name for his own, was there no one among us who could have found it out?”

“Everyone in Guangzhou who might have found it out had been killed; in Shanghai no one knew who the man being sent was, so anyone at all could use the name and, following the appointed means of contact and the passwords, make contact with Old Fang. Even within the underground Party this was top-secret; no one would think to doubt just who it was that had come.”

Because Ouyang Min had been arrested, the Guangzhou underground had been utterly wrecked, and everyone who knew of this transfer plan was gone. Ye Tao's intelligence had been exactly right: Ouyang Min had turned traitor. It was precisely his defection that let Ye Qinian learn of the plan to transfer Long Dong and grasp every detail of it — the alias, the manner of contact, the contact men. Chen Qianli guessed that Ye Qinian had not at first meant to plant Lu Zhongde for the long term, but had merely seen a fresh opportunity in what the traitor gave up.

Ye Qinian was not a man to let slip an opportunity once it was in his grasp. Many years before, when the Nationalists and Communists had only just begun to work together, he had already been ranting at gatherings of the right-wing faction within the Nationalist Party that the Communists must be torn up root and branch. So he meant to press his advantage and win one more round, laying another stake on Lu Zhongde — and the price of it was that he had Ouyang Min killed. Ouyang Min was Long Dong's superior; it was he who had arranged the plan to transfer Long Dong, and no one but he could have known it in such detail.

“The swine — too many have died at his hands: all those people in Guangzhou, Long Dong, Old Fang, and that comrade who went to the market to carry the warning. The moment I'm back I'll finish him; I'll cut out his heart and see for myself how black it is.”

And Ye Tao too, Chen Qianli thought in the silence of his heart; and perhaps Ling Wen as well — very likely she too had already been murdered by him. On the day of the Beginning of Spring they had made inquiries in the back lane of Tianguanli off Haoxian Road, and not one of the neighbors would answer them a word; seeing outsiders come in, every face turned fearful. Chen Qianli had hurried Liang Shichao away, suspecting that the people of Haoxian Road had been frightened by what happened that night. But —
“We can't kill him yet. This bullet — let him keep it on account another half-month.”
“Why?”

Because now the only man who could reach Comrade Haohan was he, and because they must find a way to draw Comrade Haohan clear of the danger closing in upon him. But this Chen Qianli could not tell Liang Shichao — not yet.

“Because we have a more important task. Not only can we not kill him for the present — we can't let him know that we already know he's a mole. At noon today he's to meet us at the Gonghexiang Wharf, and on no account must he be allowed to see through us,” he said.

That day, in the Tanka shack, he had put one question to Old Xiao: why he had meant to see Ling Wen the next day. Once that question was asked, the fog had begun to lift. On the first day of the first month, standing on the roof of the bank, he had seen Cui Wentai from afar go tearing off in the car, and a doubt had sprung up in him then and there. The visitor from the Qingdao boat had told him there was a mole in the Shanghai underground, code-named “Xi Shi.” The Special Operations Headquarters' ace planted agent, Ye Qinian's darling — could it be Cui Wentai?
He had read that newspaper, and he knew that Ling Wen, come to that street, would find no clue there either; why, then, should she have vanished?

Now he understood. Lu Zhongde had had to do away with her to get his chance at the top-secret message Old Xiao carried in his head. With Ling Wen gone, he could put on a piece of theater, deceive Old Xiao, and get Old Xiao to disclose the message to him. Once Lu Zhongde was back in Shanghai the day before, he would surely have reported to Ye Qinian at once: the sole means of reaching Comrade Haohan from the outside was now in the agents' hands. Even were Chen Qianli to return to Shanghai today, there was no possibility whatever of getting the contact signal out first, for the advertisement pages of those two newspapers would certainly be held fast in the agents' grip.

It would be a trap there was no cracking; even by force there was likely no way to intercept it. Once Comrade Haohan had dialed that number, the agents would tell him the place of the meeting — and where that place was, Chen Qianli had no means of finding out.

And so, now, not only could Lu Zhongde not be got rid of — he must be left thinking his fox's tail had not been exposed. In Guangzhou, Chen Qianli had told Mo Shaoqiu the whole of it, and had had him notify the underground to close every liaison station in Hong Kong and Guangzhou that Lu Zhongde had been in touch with. He had asked Mo Shaoqiu, too, once Old Xiao was seen to, to hasten to Ruijin as soon as he could and report it all in detail to Comrade Shaoshan, keeping safe and secret on the road. Chen Qianli hurried back from Guangzhou to Hong Kong that same night; before boarding he went once to the post office and sent a telegram to Chen Qianyuan, for his younger brother to pass the contents on to Lin Shi. The telegram said that he would arrive at the Gonghexiang Wharf aboard the Guisheng around twelve o'clock noon today, and that Yi Junnian was to come and meet him.

Chen Qianli reckoned that Lu Zhongde, back in Shanghai, would certainly go on keeping in touch with Lin Shi and the others, would put on a grieving face and tell them all the news of Ling Wen's disappearance — and might well know that Chen Qianli himself had left Shanghai, and from that suspect he had gone to Guangzhou. To cover up what Lu Zhongde had done in Guangzhou, the agents would surely want him, Chen Qianli, dead and silenced, so as to keep Lu Zhongde's identity from leaking and keep the means of reaching Haohan in their own hands. He had to make Lu Zhongde believe he had never been to Guangzhou; only so could he find his chance to throw open Ye Qinian's trap and save Comrade Haohan.

He guessed the agents would have made their preparations, and that the moment he appeared they would move at once to kill him. But if he went of his own accord to meet Lu Zhongde, it might leave the man trusting to luck, believing he could go on deceiving heaven and crossing the sea. In that case, Chen Qianli reckoned, the agents would lay a double plan — ready both to kill him and to have Lu Zhongde go on playing Yi Junnian. At the meeting on the wharf, one careless move on his part and the agents might well strike at once; somewhere, perhaps, on a rooftop beside the wharf a marksman lay hidden, waiting for Lu Zhongde's signal. He meant to put on a piece of theater for Lu Zhongde in his turn, to lull him, to make him think they knew nothing at all of what had happened in Guangzhou — that they had never been to Guangzhou, had never met Mo Shaoqiu or Old Xiao, and knew nothing of Ling Wen's sudden disappearance.

The Guisheng came in across the mouth of the Wusong River at fifty minutes past ten in the morning, a quarter-hour past the top of the tide. After only half an hour's wait the pilot came up on deck and conned the ship into port. Just after twelve o'clock, Liang Shichao, standing on deck, caught sight of the Gonghexiang Wharf. The jetty berth for large ships was already occupied, and the Guisheng could only lie at anchor in midstream; the steamship company had hired a small steam-lighter to ferry the passengers ashore. Such a lighter had a broad deck platform, and once it came alongside the great ship let down her gangway, so that the passengers, going down, stepped straight onto the lighter to be carried across to land. Passengers with much luggage might wait on the wharf, or leave ahead and entrust a travel agency to deliver their baggage to their homes.
Chen Qianli told Liang Shichao not to go ashore yet, but to wait until he himself had landed before leaving.

The steam-lighter drew slowly in to the bank. This lot it carried were all first- and second-class passengers, standing about the deck by twos and threes, well dressed and all smiles, with none of the weariness and tedium of a long voyage upon them. When the ropes had been made fast at either end, a bell sounded in the bows and the gate in the rail was opened.

The day Chen Qianli left Shanghai wind and snow had driven together; he came back to bright sunshine and the first look of early spring. The jetty was an upward-sloping ramp; the Gonghexiang Wharf had been rebuilt two or three years before, and the planks of the jetty had a great spring to them, thudding underfoot as one walked. Off the jetty and ashore stood the Gonghexiang Wharf Company, with rows of sedan cars parked on the open ground, and the crowd come to meet the arrivals standing on either side of the jetty.

He saw Lu Zhongde, but marked nothing amiss around him. The agents were most likely hidden in the cars, and in some corner of the roof of the wharf company's three-story building a marksman perhaps lay in wait. He knew Ye Qinian: if the man had resolved on silencing him to keep Lu Zhongde planted, he would choose just such a clean, direct way. Chen Qianli guessed these agents must be trusted men Ye Qinian had brought up specially from the Special Operations Headquarters in Nanjing, the better to keep Lu Zhongde's secret from leaking. He would have picked them with great care — so their marksmanship, too, would surely be very good.

He walked on toward the gate on the right of the wharf building, and not very fast — as at any such meeting, letting the other man come up on him slowly from behind and to the side. Now they were abreast.
“Is there any way to get hold of a boat?” he asked Lu Zhongde.
“A boat?”
“I want to hire a small cargo boat, two or three hundred tons, one that can carry freight — and, better still, carry a few other things too. What I really want is the passenger cabin aboard her.”
“To what use?”

“To carry someone off. An unremarkable little cargo boat, loaded with rice and sugar and bolts of cloth, or some other goods. An old boat that draws no notice, but well enough found to stand the wind and waves at sea.” He spoke as he thought, as though the idea had come to him only minutes before — just as he landed and saw those cranes towering by the river's edge, or once ashore caught sight of the words “Warehouse: Restricted” on a distant wall; it seemed that even as he spoke and thought, the notion was only now taking shape.
“You had me come down to the wharf just for this?”

“Arrange me a place to put up. It seems now that hotels are no longer safe. For the next few days I want somewhere secret and reliable. Best if the house is on the larger side — during the days of the operation we may need to lodge several people.”
“That's no trouble. When do you want it?”
“Today.”

Chen Qianli felt the other man relax a little; perhaps his words had told. He did not look about him, but he knew the agents must have their eyes fixed on the two of them. The wharf company's gate stood open, its iron leaves lettered in Chinese and English: “No Admittance Except on Business.” At the gate stood two or three children, holding out big biscuit-tins in their hands, and in the tins all sorts of cigarettes and small change.

Outside the gate was East Broadway. Down one side of the road stood the wharf companies one after another — Shuntai, the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company, Wayside, the Japan Mail Steamship Company, the Yehsong Dockyard. A tramline ran down the middle of the road, and the shops on the far side were all houses that did business with the ships: hardware-and-parts shops, cigarette-and-paper shops, shoe-and-hat shops, foreign-money exchange shops, and a great many bars besides — the second floors of some of them not only curtained but with every pane pasted over in patterned paper, as though those rooms had the greatest need of dimness.

Chen Qianli wondered: should he tell him a little more? He drew Lu Zhongde into a small café that sold, among other things, fried pork chops and borscht. The pork chop had been let go cold and then fried a second time, and the borscht looked more than a little doubtful. But then neither of them had any interest in the food. Chen Qianli looked out of the window and saw Liang Shichao come out of the wharf company's gate and vanish into the milling crowd. He turned his head to face Lu Zhongde, and found the man staring at him.
“Comrade Ling Wen has disappeared.”
Lu Zhongde said it suddenly. Chen Qianli did not show any great surprise — yet neither could he seem to have known of it all along. He was checked a moment —
“Where?”
“In Guangzhou. Did you not know?”
Chen Qianli shook his head, like a man who has just heard some dreadful piece of news and whose mind has not yet come round to it.
“I thought Lin Shi would have told you in the telegram.” Lu Zhongde added the words softly, forcing out a trace of grief.
“What happened?”

Lu Zhongde was silent a good while. Chen Qianli listened to the man's answers, holding down the anger in his heart. He knew Lu Zhongde must have had his story ready long before; he himself was just as ready — that whatever the man said, he would feign not the least suspicion.

Lu Zhongde said that Ling Wen had gone to the newspaper offices, and then to the Guangzhou Press Association's clipping bureau. She had insisted on going to Haoxian Road — what was the name of that back lane? He made a show of asking himself, and then answered: the back lane of Tianguanli. Chen Qianli had not expected him to say so; in Guangzhou it was not thus that he had spoken to Mo Shaoqiu — there he had said they had never been to Haoxian Road. Was Lu Zhongde, then, deliberately leaving a flaw showing, to test him and see how he would react?

Lu Zhongde said he had wanted to stop her; he said, with vexation, that had he known it would come to this he would have held her back with all his might. From this he ventured a mild word of criticism against the leadership above him: since the Guangzhou trip had been settled as Comrade Ling Wen's charge, there were times when it was not for him to say much. After all, the underground Party had strict rules of discipline between higher and lower ranks, and a subordinate ought not to inquire too closely into a superior's thinking and doings. Comrade Ling Wen need not, indeed, have told him where she meant to go. He had waited a long time, and deep into the night she still had not come back.

At first light he had hurried to Haoxian Road, and searched that back lane a good long while before finding he had gone wrong: he should have turned right under a great banyan tree instead of going straight on — for the back lane had to be reckoned by the lie of Haoxian Road, and since Haoxian Road ran along the south, the back lane must be at the far north, not on eastward along that straight alley. With all this delay, the day had come full light.

But the back lane was still empty of people; he saw only an old fortune-teller, who for some reason was sitting out in the street so early, and who caught at him and would tell his fortune. He asked the old fortune-teller whether, the afternoon before, he had seen a strange woman come into the lane to ask after certain things — a woman of thirty or so. He had meant to tell the old man she was in a cheongsam and a woolen sweater, but thinking the old man was not likely to remember such things, he changed his mind and said simply that she was finely dressed, very handsome — very leng.

The boat would not sail till evening, so he still had time to go once to the liaison station at the Xingchang Apothecary. The station was in the charge of Mo Shaoqiu, and there was a Mrs. Mo besides; it was Mrs. Mo who had told Ling Wen about the newspaper, and so he meant to look in at the station. But no sooner had he reached Jianglan Street than he felt something was wrong: there were plainclothesmen in the street, and though the plainclothes agents of Guangzhou dressed unlike those of Shanghai, the look and bearing of these petty agents could be told at a glance. Sure enough, before long the street fell into confusion and someone opened fire. Judging that something had gone amiss at the liaison station, he could only make off in haste. He went back to the hotel and waited until evening, and still Ling Wen did not appear; there was nothing for it but to board the boat back to Shanghai, for the task was too important and he could wait no longer.
